passage: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely
text:
The selected phrase means the Transformer does away with recurrent and convolutional layers altogether.

The sentence says the proposed model is built only from attention mechanisms and drops the two common building blocks of earlier sequence models: recurrence, where each step depends on the previous hidden state (as in LSTMs and GRUs), and convolutions, which look at fixed-size local windows. Instead, every position in the sequence is related to every other directly through attention p. 2.

Here, "recurrence" means processing tokens one after another, which blocks parallel computation, and "convolution" means sliding a small filter across the input. Removing both lets the model process all positions at once, which the authors credit for its speed and parallelism p. 1.

passage: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples
text:
The passage argues that recurrent models must process a sequence one step at a time, so their computation cannot be split up across positions within a single training example.

The sentence is the conclusion of the preceding explanation: each hidden state h_t depends on the previous one h_{t-1} and the input at position t, so step t cannot begin until step t-1 finishes. This is what the authors mean by "sequential nature" p. 2. Parallelization means doing many of these computations at once on parallel hardware such as GPUs.

Here the point sets up the paper's motivation. The authors say this constraint becomes critical for longer sequences, because memory limits restrict how many examples can be batched together, and the Transformer is proposed to avoid the sequential dependency p. 2.

The passage says recurrent networks, especially LSTM and gated recurrent networks, were firmly established as state of the art in sequence modeling and transduction p. 2. That matched the field in 2017. From about 2018 onward, Transformer models displaced recurrent networks in machine translation and language modeling, and the same architecture underlies BERT and the GPT family. card:
Fact-check · p. 10
×
the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based on recurrent or convolutional layers

Partly holds. The claim was supported by the paper's own experiments, but as a general statement it depends on the setting.

The paper's evidence is specific. Its base model took about 12 hours on eight P100 GPUs, and the big model took 3.5 days on the same hardware p. 7. Its translation results are described as coming at a fraction of the training cost of competing models p. 8. Those costs were partly estimated from GPU time and assumed sustained FLOPS per GPU p. 8, so "significantly faster" rests on comparisons against specific 2016 to 2017 recurrent and convolutional systems, not on a universal speed measurement. The original paper's own abstract makes the same point about training time on two translation tasks, and the Google Research blog summary repeats the claim with a speedup of up to an order of magnitude (Google Research, 2017). Later practice has also reshaped the picture: the Transformer's parallelism became the basis for large-scale training, but its cost grows quadratically with sequence length, which the paper itself flagged as a future concern p. 7. A more recent comparative study reported Transformers training slower than some RNN and CNN models in its own benchmark (ResearchGate, 2025), so the result is not uniform across tasks, hardware, or sequence lengths. That study is a single secondary source, so I weigh it lightly.

Note. The passage describes the paper's own results, which the paper reports accurately. It does not establish the Transformer as faster to train in every setting, and that broader reading is what has been challenged.

self-attention could yield more interpretable models

Partly holds. The paper's hedged claim that self-attention could aid interpretability is a reasonable hypothesis, but attention weights alone have not proven to be reliable explanations p. 7.

Partly holds. The paper does not test interpretability. It offers the point as a side benefit and points to attention distributions in the appendix as illustration only p. 7. The appendix figures show heads that seem tied to anaphora and to sentence structure pp. 14–15, which is suggestive but qualitative. Later work has largely cautioned against reading raw attention weights as explanations. Brunner et al. (2020) report that attention weights are not directly interpretable and propose complementary tools, and Sun and Marasović (2021) show that only part of the attention matrix contributes to outputs, so conventional attention maps can mislead interpretability analyses. Mohankumar et al. (2020) argue that attention distributions are often neither faithful nor plausible explanations, though their evidence concerns LSTM encoders.

Note. Interpretability has since been pursued through other routes, such as effective attention, attribution methods and probing, rather than through attention maps alone. The original paper's claim should be read as an early hypothesis, not an established finding.

passage: Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks
text:
Path length is only one factor in learning long-range dependencies, so treating shorter paths as the key remedy overstates what self-attention gains.

A careful critic would argue that a short path does not guarantee a strong or selective signal along it. Self-attention connects every pair of positions in a single step, but each output is a weighted average over all positions, so the contribution of a distant token can be diluted among many others. The document itself acknowledges this trade-off, describing reduced effective resolution caused by averaging attention-weighted positions p. 2. On this view, maximum path length measures connectivity in the network, not whether the relevant dependency can actually be isolated and learned.

The author's best reply is that path length is offered as one of three desiderata alongside computational complexity and parallelism, and that the averaging cost is countered by multi-head attention, which lets the model attend to different representation subspaces at different positions p. 2.

question: Why use 8 smaller heads instead of one big attention head?
text:
The document gives two reasons, and one of them is stated only briefly. The first is on the page you're reading: multi-head attention lets the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, whereas with a single head, averaging inhibits this p. 5. In other words, one head produces one set of weights and one weighted average, so it has to blend everything it finds relevant into a single mixture. Separate heads, each with its own learned projections, can look for different things at once.

The second is cost. Each head uses dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64, so the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality p. 5. Splitting costs roughly nothing extra.

The earlier background section also describes multi-head attention as the remedy for the reduced effective resolution caused by averaging attention-weighted positions p. 2.

For evidence, the ablation shows that single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, though quality also drops with too many heads p. 9. The document doesn't explain why 8 in particular works well; it reports that result empirically.

question: What is label smoothing, and why would it help BLEU while hurting perplexity?
text:
The document does not define label smoothing beyond its value, ε_ls = 0.1, and a citation to Szegedy et al. p. 8. What follows about the mechanism is general knowledge, not something the paper explains.

In standard training, the target for each token is a one-hot distribution: probability 1 on the correct word, 0 everywhere else. Label smoothing replaces that with a softened target, where the correct word gets slightly less than 1 (roughly 1 minus ε) and the remaining ε is spread across the other vocabulary items. So the model is penalized for being extremely confident.

The perplexity effect follows directly from this. Perplexity measures how much probability the model puts on the correct token, and a model trained to hold back some probability mass will assign lower probability to the right answer than an overconfident one would. That is what the paper means by "the model learns to be more unsure" p. 8.

Why BLEU improves is not explained in the document. The paper only reports that accuracy and BLEU improve. A common explanation is that preventing overconfidence acts as regularization and gives better-calibrated scores during beam search, but that is an outside interpretation, not a claim made here.

passage: We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings
question: If learned embeddings performed the same, why keep the sinusoids?
text:
The document gives one reason, stated right after the comparison: "We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training." p. 6 A learned embedding table only has entries for the positions seen in training, whereas a sinusoid is a fixed function that can be evaluated at any position.

The authors also offer a second motivation earlier, though it applies to sinusoids in general rather than as a tiebreaker. They hypothesized the sinusoids would make it easy to attend by relative position, since for any fixed offset k, the encoding at pos+k is a linear function of the encoding at pos. p. 6

Note the wording is hedged ("may allow"). The paper does not test extrapolation to longer sequences, so that benefit is a rationale rather than something the experiments demonstrate. The only evidence offered is that the learned version gave nearly identical results, with a dev BLEU of 25.7 against 25.8 for the base model. p. 9

question: What does a beam size of 4 mean in practice?
text:
The document does not explain beam search itself; it only states the settings: a beam size of 4 and length penalty α = 0.6, chosen after experimentation on the development set p. 8. What follows is general background, not something the paper says.

In beam search, the decoder does not commit to a single best word at each step. Because the Transformer generates output one token at a time, conditioned on earlier tokens p. 2, it can keep several partial translations alive at once. With a beam size of 4, it holds the 4 highest-scoring partial outputs. At each step it extends each of them by one token, scores all the resulting candidates, and keeps only the best 4. This continues until the hypotheses finish, and the best finished one is returned.

A beam of 1 would be greedy decoding. Larger beams search more thoroughly but cost more computation, and they tend to favor shorter outputs, which is why a length penalty like α is applied. The paper also notes a larger beam of 21 for parsing p. 10.

question: What limitations of the Transformer do the authors themselves acknowledge?
text:
The paper has no dedicated limitations section, so what follows is scattered admissions and stated future work.

Reduced resolution: the constant number of operations between any two positions comes "at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions," which multi-head attention is meant to counteract p. 2.

Long sequences: self-attention is cheaper than recurrence only when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimension d. For very long inputs the authors propose restricting attention to a neighborhood of size r, and they leave that for future work p. 7. The document never uses the word "quadratic," so reading this as a quadratic cost is my own inference from the complexity comparison p. 6.

The attention scoring function: shrinking dk hurts quality, which the authors take to suggest that "a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may be beneficial" p. 9. Quality also drops with too many heads p. 9.

Sequential generation: the decoder is auto-regressive p. 2, and the conclusion lists "making generation less sequential" as a goal p. 10.

Scope: extending the model to images, audio and video is listed as a plan, not a result p. 10. On parsing, the model beat all earlier reported models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar p. 10.

question: Which ablation results in Table 3 matter most, and why?
text:
Table 3 is on page 9, and the paper itself singles out a few rows. I'd rank them this way.

Row (A), heads: single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, but quality also drops with too many heads p. 9. With computation held constant, this is the main evidence for multi-head attention, and it shows a sweet spot (the base choice of 8 heads, dk = 64, scores 25.8 BLEU against 24.9 for one head) p. 9.

Row (B), smaller dk: reducing the key size hurts quality. The authors read this as a sign that "determining compatibility is not easy" and that a better function than dot product may help p. 9. This is the one result that points to a weakness in their design.

Rows (C) and (D), size and dropout: bigger models are better, and dropout is "very helpful in avoiding over-fitting" p. 9. These are expected results, but they justify the big configuration.

Row (E): learned positional embeddings give 25.7 BLEU against 25.8 for sinusoids, nearly identical p. 9. The authors chose sinusoids because they may extrapolate to longer sequences p. 6. The document does not test that claim.

One caveat: the table's text is garbled in places, and some row labels (such as which values changed in rows B and C) are missing, so I'm relying on the paper's own description of each row.

Before you start
×

The paper proposes the Transformer, a translation architecture built only on attention, with no recurrence or convolution. It matters because it aims for better quality and far faster parallel training, and the rest of the paper describes, motivates and tests that design.

Key claims

1
The Transformer relies entirely on attention to draw global dependencies between input and output, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions. p. 2
2
Self-attention relates any two positions in a constant number of sequential operations, versus O(n) for recurrent layers. p. 6
3
The big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, beating prior results including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. p. 8
4
Ablations show single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads. p. 9
5
A 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning performs well on English constituency parsing, including with only 40K WSJ training sentences. p. 10

Keep in mind

The English-to-French big model score appears as 41.8 in the abstract and Table 2 but as 41.0 in the text of section 6.1. Check which figure you rely on.
Attention itself is not new. The novelty claimed is using it without recurrent or convolutional layers, so read the Background section with that distinction in mind.
Perplexities in Table 3 are per-wordpiece under byte-pair encoding, so they should not be compared with per-word perplexities from other work. Training cost figures are estimates built from GPU time and assumed sustained TFLOPS.
